Belgium: national strike against De Wever's cuts, no passenger flights in Brussels and Charleroi this Monday as air traffic controllers join the action

This Monday, November 23, Belgium's three main unions are marching in Brussels against the austerity measures of Bart De Wever's government. With Skeyes air traffic controllers joining the strike, the country's two main airports have almost no commercial flights from 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. [1][3][4].

Skeyes, the public body that runs air traffic control, warned it could not provide normal service at airports or in Belgian airspace between 7 a.m. and 9 p.m. local time, because some of its controllers are on strike [1][4].

Brussels Airport announced the cancellation of all departing and arriving passenger flights this Monday [3]. Charleroi Airport, for its part, warned of a complete closure of all the country's airports for the day [4].

The ACV-CSC, ABVV-FGTB and ACLVB unions are calling for a national demonstration: gathering at 10 a.m. at Brussels-North station, speeches, then departure around 11 a.m. toward Brussels-South station [2]. Students have announced they will join the march [2].
The unions denounce measures affecting pensions, working conditions and purchasing power [1]. Public transport is also disrupted [1].
Flemish nationalist Prime Minister Bart De Wever (N-VA) has been negotiating for months with his partners over a €10 billion savings budget spread over the coming years [1].
In early November, lacking agreement within his coalition, he offered his resignation; King Philippe refused it and gave him more time to find a solution [1].
Key takeaway: by closing Belgian skies for 14 hours, the strike shows that opposition to budget cuts can paralyze a country that hosts the European institutions [1][4].

The movement has been going on for months. At the previous national demonstration, on March 12, 2026, police counted about 80,000 people in Brussels, unions more than 100,000 [5]. No turnout figure was yet known for this Monday at the time of writing.

For the government, the dilemma is the same as in many European countries: cutting the deficit without crushing purchasing power. The €10 billion budget still has to be finalized by a coalition that already nearly collapsed this month [1].
Belgium is not alone: as recently as November 21, marches against the high cost of living and inequality took place in Portugal, Spain and France [6].

If you were due to fly from Brussels or Charleroi this Monday, your flight is very likely cancelled: check with your airline, which must offer you a refund or another flight. Belgian trains and buses are also disrupted, including services to France.

Ukraine: a Russian drone rips open an apartment building near Kyiv, at least six dead and 14 missing, including two children, at the end of a week of 2,700 drones

During the night of November 21 to 22, a Russian drone destroyed part of a five-story apartment building in Dymer, north of Kyiv. Rescuers are still searching the rubble: at least six dead and 14 to 15 missing according to the latest tolls. Zelensky points out that no security guarantees exist on paper yet [1][2][4][7].
The drone hit a five-story residential building in Dymer, a small town in the Vyshhorod district, north of the capital [1][3].

The first toll from Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv regional military administration, reported two bodies pulled from the rubble and four injured [2]. Subsequent tolls rose to six dead on Monday [4], and the Kyiv Independent counts at least seven [3].
“Unfortunately, people may still be trapped under the rubble: 14 people remain unaccounted for,” Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on X, after nine residents were evacuated [1][2].
Ukraine's National Police later counted 15 missing, “including two children: an 11-year-old girl and a 7-year-old boy” [2].

That night, Russia launched 186 long-range attack drones, 72 of them jet-powered; the Ukrainian air force says it shot down or neutralized 161, according to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) [5].

Over the week, Russia targeted 20 Ukrainian regions with about 2,700 drones, nearly 1,460 aerial bombs and 165 missiles, according to Zelensky [2][3]. On the Russian side, Moscow says it shot down 170 Ukrainian drones the same night; Kyiv struck military infrastructure in the Krasnodar region [5].
Key takeaway: strikes on residential buildings continue at the same pace while American, European, Ukrainian and Russian envoys discuss a peace plan [3][7].

On the substance of the negotiations, nothing is signed: Volodymyr Zelensky acknowledged that no draft security guarantees existed on paper yet, and is demanding guarantees that last far longer than a US presidential term, ideally “forever” [7].

On November 20, he called NATO and EU membership the “best security guarantee” and proposed four-way negotiations: Ukraine, Europe, the United States and Russia [8]. Moscow has not responded to this proposal in the available sources.

For Europe, the stakes are direct: Zelensky wants Europeans at the table, on an equal footing with Washington and Moscow, because the security of the whole continent depends on the outcome of these talks [8].

Every night of massive strikes is a reminder that the war is not over, despite the negotiations. For Europe, this means military spending that keeps climbing and aid to Ukraine that weighs on national budgets, including France's.

news.2026-11-23-prefet-moutouh-fuites-rn: Alleged leaks to the RN: prefect Hugues Moutouh, former number two at the Interior Ministry, asks to leave his post; Marine Le Pen says she “never received anything”

Suspected of having tipped off the Rassemblement National about investigations targeting it, Hugues Moutouh, prefect of the Centre-Val de Loire region and former secretary general of the Interior Ministry, asked on Saturday to be relieved of his duties. He denounces a “manhunt”. Marine Le Pen denies any exchange of information [1][3][5].

On Saturday, November 21, in Orléans, Hugues Moutouh, prefect of the Centre-Val de Loire region and of the Loiret, asked to be relieved of his duties, the day after being summoned by Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez [5][6].

A judicial investigation has been open since July 27 by the Paris prosecutor's office for breach of professional secrecy, breach of investigative secrecy and handling the proceeds of these offenses [6].
At the heart of the case: an email from the Interior Ministry's general secretariat, which the prefect had headed since 2025, concerning judicial investigations targeting the RN [1][2].

The message was found during a search of the Rome home of Frédéric Chatillon, a close associate of Marine Le Pen who long managed the party's election communications, as part of a separate case brought by the European Public Prosecutor's Office [1][2].
The Interior Ministry itself was searched in late July [6]. “If the facts are proven, they are very serious,” said Laurent Nuñez [6].
Hugues Moutouh disputes this: he says he acted in accordance with the law and political neutrality, and speaks of a “manhunt” [1][6].

On Sunday, November 22, Marine Le Pen, head of the RN group in the National Assembly, insisted she had “never received confidential information” from him nor “ever asked” for any. “I don't know him personally,” she added [3][4].
Key takeaway: the suspicion reaches the heart of the state, since a former administrative number two at the Interior Ministry may have informed a party under judicial investigation [1][2].

The ministry's secretary general oversees an administration that runs the police, elections and prefectures. An email leaving this office and found at the home of someone close to a party is therefore taken very seriously, even though no formal charges are known at this stage [1][6].
The prefect is no unknown: as head of the Alpes-Maritimes, he earned the nickname “bulldozer prefect” [6]. His departure was not yet official on Saturday evening [6].

The affair comes a few months before the 2027 presidential election, in which the RN starts in a strong position: it forces the party to defend itself on integrity, and the government to show that the administration remains neutral [3][4].

Prefects and senior Interior Ministry officials must be neutral: they are the ones who organize elections. An investigation into leaks to a party, whichever it is, therefore touches on trust in the vote. Nothing has been proven: the courts still have to establish the facts.

AI chips diverted to China: Washington is still waiting for Nvidia's answers, and Scott Bessent refuses to back the return of Jensen Huang that Trump wants

On Sunday, November 22, on CBS, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the administration still had not received the answers it demanded from Nvidia about AI chips that ended up in China. He wants to know who was in charge of controls and does not support the return of Jensen Huang, who resigned on November 12 [1][3][7].

“We need answers,” Scott Bessent said on “Face the Nation”. The Treasury is in contact with Nvidia's interim leadership, its lead directors and its lawyers, but has not received what it asked for a week ago [1][2].
He had then demanded answers “within the next ten days” from the board of directors and outside counsel [1].
“We need to see who was in charge of compliance,” he said, meaning compliance with export rules, and “at what level of the company” people knew about the diversions [1].

On a return of Jensen Huang to the head of the group, he replied: “I think we need to see where the buck stops” [3][4]. On Friday, however, Donald Trump had called Huang a “good man” who “made bad decisions”, and said he wanted him back [11].

The scandal stems from Alice Huang, a former executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore company suspected by US intelligence of spying for China [9]. Bessent considers this aspect “a bit of a red herring”: “I assume he didn't know she was an alleged spy” [3].

Bessent asked why the Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, had not blacklisted Megaspeed: “Treasury and several other departments called for it” [1][4]. Nvidia had removed Megaspeed from its customer list in August 2025, according to him [4].

The Justice and Commerce departments are conducting a criminal investigation into Megaspeed, whose boss Tan Yong Pong denies any wrongdoing [9]. The stock market regulator (SEC) is also examining Nvidia's accounting, an early-stage investigation that may close without charges [6].

Key takeaway: the Nvidia affair is no longer just a corporate scandal, it is a matter of state about controlling sensitive technologies sold to China, and the US government is speaking with several voices on it [1][5].

On one side, Donald Trump wants Jensen Huang back [11]; on the other, his Treasury Secretary first wants to know who knew what. On November 15, Bessent was already wondering whether Nvidia had “inflated” its results with suspicious sales in China [5].

The context makes the question pressing: on November 19, a House of Representatives committee revealed that Commerce had authorized 879,868 Nvidia and AMD AI chips for Chinese buyers in six months [10].
At Nvidia, chief financial officer Colette Kress has been acting as interim leader since Huang's departure, and the board is looking for a successor, both internally and externally [8].

Nvidia carries a very heavy weight in the major stock indices, and therefore in many savings and pension funds, including in Europe. As long as Washington does not have its answers, the risk of a penalty or new restrictions keeps hanging over the group.

Chile: Kast's approval rises to 23%, but a right-wing senator accuses him of being out of touch and marches against his government begin Tuesday

According to the Criteria poll published on Sunday, November 22, 23% of Chileans approve of President José Antonio Kast, five points more than before, against 68% who disapprove. The same day, Senator Manuel José Ossandón criticized his lack of “sintonía” (connection) with the population, and organizations announced marches starting Tuesday [1][2][3].
The Criteria poll shows approval up five points, to 23%, and disapproval down, to 68% [3][4]. This rebound follows a collapse in the president's rating in recent weeks [3].
The best-rated ministers are Iván Poduje and May Chomali, with 48% favorable opinions each, double the president's figure [4].
Manuel José Ossandón, senator for Renovación Nacional (RN), gave a harsh assessment: “It has been hard for him to get in tune with people's problems” [1].

He also criticizes Kast for backing minister Fernando Rabat, whom he believes should have been removed from the government [1]. A constitutional accusation, a procedure that can lead to a minister's removal, targets Fernando Rabat [2].
The undersecretary for Science, Carolina Rossi, has resigned: this is the second departure from that post since the start of the term [2].
In the presidential camp, deputy José Meza defends the record and says the country remains under an “emergency government”; the majority turns the criticism back on the opposition [2].
Organizations have announced a series of marches against the government starting Tuesday, November 24 [2].
Key takeaway: despite a slight improvement in the polls, more than two in three Chileans disapprove of their president, and criticism now also comes from the right [1][3].

Last week, Kast was touring three Asian countries and attending the APEC summit [4]. On November 20 in Tokyo, he offered Chile's critical minerals to Japan [5]. But on the home front, the departure of a second undersecretary for Science and the proceedings against a minister are weakening his team [2].
The gap between a president at 23% and two ministers at 48% [4] shows that Chileans judge the head of state more harshly than some of his policies.
The street will be the next test: the size of the marches announced from Tuesday will show whether the discontent measured in the polls turns into mobilization [2].

Chile is offering its critical minerals to wealthy countries, as it did with Japan on November 20 [5]. A weakened government and social tensions can slow the reforms and mining projects that European manufacturers are also following closely.

Uruguay: the PIT-CNT union federation loses the workers' seat at the head of social security for the first time, a historic defeat

In the elections to the Social Security Bank (BPS) on Sunday, November 22, Lorena Roqueta's “Hay otro camino” list beat that of the PIT-CNT union federation to represent workers. According to an Electoral Court count, it won 451,304 votes against 370,377. A first, as the PIT-CNT had won every previous vote [1][4][7].
On Sunday, Uruguayans elected the “social directors” of the BPS, the public social security body: workers and retirees each choose a representative on its board [1][8].

Among workers, Lorena Roqueta (list 15, “Hay otro camino”, “There is another way”) is ahead of Carlos Clavijo (list 11, PIT-CNT): 451,304 votes against 370,377 according to an official Electoral Court count [7]. Another tally, by the daily La Diaria, gives 436,815 against 356,712 [1].

This is the first time the PIT-CNT has lost a BPS election; it had won in 2006, 2011, 2016 and 2021 [1]. Several media outlets speak of a defeat unprecedented in 34 years and of the “end of a hegemony” [4][5].
Among retirees, Estela Ovelar, of the ONAJPU organization, was narrowly ahead of Renaldo Borriero, a result not yet confirmed [6][7].
The PIT-CNT and ONAJPU have filed complaints with the Electoral Court over irregularities in the distribution of ballots [1].
President Yamandú Orsi voted early at School 110 in Canelones. He said he was “convinced of the importance of taking care of institutions” and hailed “an expression of our democracy” [8][9].
The final count is due to begin on Tuesday, November 24 [6].
Key takeaway: the PIT-CNT, Uruguay's main union federation, loses the workers' seat on the social security board for the first time, after four consecutive victories [1][3][5].
This defeat touches a sensitive subject: the BPS leadership takes part in decisions on social security, and it is now a rival list that will carry workers' voices there [1][2].

The result has yet to be confirmed: the complaints filed over irregularities and the final count, starting Tuesday, could still shift the numbers, especially among retirees where the gap is very narrow [1][6].

Uruguay, like France, is debating the future of its pensions. The fact that workers preferred a list other than the big national union's shows that union federations no longer necessarily speak for all workers, a question that also arises in Europe.

Taiwan bans almost all short selling after its worst week in more than 30 years, and its $15 billion state fund is buying shares

After its worst week in more than 30 years, Taiwan is bringing out the big guns. Since Monday, November 23, the financial regulator has banned short selling of any stock that fell the previous day, and tightened the conditions for these bets on falling prices. Its state fund of 500 billion Taiwan dollars, about $15 billion, has been buying shares since November 6 [3][4][5].
On Friday, November 20, the Taiex index plunged 6.23%, to 36,033.29 points [2]. TSMC, the island's largest company, lost 4.76%, according to the Taipei Times [1].
Over the week, Taiwanese stocks fell 17%, their biggest weekly drop since 1990 according to Reuters [4], since 1991 according to other media [3].

Since Monday, the Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) has banned short selling of any stock that fell in the previous session. The ban covers both margin short sales and sales of borrowed shares [3][5].

Securities and futures firms that short sell for hedging are exempt [3][12]. The minimum collateral required for a short sale rises from 130% to 150%, and the FSC is no longer accepting new put “warrants” [3].

This rule replaces Thursday's, which only covered stocks down 3.5% or more. Already on November 9, the FSC had lowered the share of intraday short selling allowed from 30% to 3% [3]. It has set no end date [3].
The National Financial Stabilization Fund, endowed with 500 billion Taiwan dollars, about $15 billion, has been buying shares since November 6 [3].

TSMC has lost 590 Taiwan dollars, or 22.78%, since its October high of 2,590 [1]. Retail investors are taking the opportunity to buy its shares in small lots [1]. The group also said it would comply with the new US chip rules [7].

Key takeaway: Taiwan makes a large share of the world's most advanced chips, mainly through TSMC. Its stock market is the AI barometer. When Wall Street doubts AI, Taipei takes a very hard hit: −17% in one week [4].

Banning short selling aims to break the spiral: when prices fall, investors bet on further declines, which deepens the drop and scares other sellers. By blocking these bets on stocks that are already falling, Taiwan wants to slow the slide [3][5].

But the measure has a cost. Short sellers always end up buying back the shares they sold: they are also buyers during downturns. And a market where you can no longer bet on a decline can worry large foreign funds.

Taiwan is used to this: its stabilization fund has intervened ten times since 2000, which allows it to support the market without officially talking about a crisis, notes The Korea Times [8]. Past cases show, however, that it is not always enough to reverse the trend [11].

TSMC is in almost every global and technology fund. If you own one, Taiwan's −17% week showed up in it. Government measures can slow a fall, but they don't change the fundamentals: if doubts about AI persist, prices can fall further.

How it works: short selling, and why it gets banned in a crash

Short selling means betting on a decline. The investor borrows a share, say at 100, and sells it right away. If the price falls to 80, they buy it back, return it to the lender and keep 20 in profit. If it rises, they lose. In a sharp fall, these bets can accelerate the decline. That is why Taiwan now bans short selling of a stock that fell the previous day, and requires collateral of 150% of the value sold, up from 130% before [3]. The downside: short sellers have to buy back one day, and those purchases often support rebounds. Without them, a market can become less liquid.

news.2026-11-23-danemark-expulse-attache: Denmark: Russian military attaché expelled and non-essential visas suspended, after an alleged plot to kill a Ukrainian rapper

Copenhagen is giving the Russian defense attaché seven days to leave the country and suspending non-essential visas for Russians. Danish intelligence accuses Moscow of organizing a plan to assassinate the Ukrainian-American rapper Kyivstoner. The Russian embassy denounces accusations without evidence [1][2][3].
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen summoned Russian ambassador Vladimir Barbin to announce the expulsion; the attaché has seven days to leave [1][2].

According to police, three men were intercepted near the venue before a concert by the rapper on September 25, north of Copenhagen [4]. For Rasmus Kieffer-Kristensen, head of the domestic intelligence service (PET), the plan was “clearly” planned by the Russian services [4].
Two Danes remain in custody; they deny the charges [1]. The Russian embassy remains open, but Copenhagen is suspending non-essential visas for Russian citizens [3].
Key takeaway: this is a rare response, targeting both a diplomat and Russians' travel, and it adds to the list of hybrid actions that Europeans attribute to Moscow [2][3].
The Russian embassy in Copenhagen rejects the accusations and says Denmark has presented no evidence [1].
The Nordic countries are taking a tougher line on Russia: expulsions, visas, border controls. For a European traveler, nothing changes, but tension between the EU and Moscow rises another notch.

news.2026-11-23-japon-entreprises-terres: Japan: cut off from Chinese rare earths, Mitsubishi Materials and Toyota Tsusho revive an industry abandoned in the 1990s

Faced with Chinese restrictions, Japanese manufacturers are rebuilding a rare earth supply chain independent of China, the Nikkei reported on November 22: recycling, refining and mining rights abroad. Japan had largely exited the sector in the 1990s [1].

Proterial and Mitsubishi Materials are seeking to refine, recycle and obtain mining rights outside China. Mitsubishi Materials has relaunched rare earth recycling, and Toyota Tsusho wants to expand rare metal recycling [1].
Refining remains the main bottleneck, as China controls most of the world's capacity [1].
Rare-earth-rich mud has been found on the Pacific seabed, near the island of Minamitorishima [1].
Beijing has added 20 Japanese companies to its export ban list: 40 are now on it, and 40 others face tighter controls [2].

Key takeaway: Chinese pressure is pushing Japan to recreate an industry it had left to China [1]. In the first half of 2026, Chinese rare earth exports to Japan fell 51% year on year, three times more than China's overall exports (−16%) [3].
Dependence remains high: in 2024, 63% of the rare earth metals imported by Japan came from China [4]. The challenge: scale up before the next shock [1].
Rare earths are used in magnets for electric cars and electronics. If Japan succeeds, Europe, which also depends on China, will have a model.
